analysis.one_liner: Excludes greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane from Clean Air Act regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act to say that carbon dioxide, water vapor, methane, and chlorofluorocarbons are not air pollutants, and that nothing in the law allows the federal government to regulate climate change or global warming. This would have barred the Environmental Protection Agency from using its existing Clean Air Act authority to limit greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, factories, and vehicles. The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Large emitters of greenhouse gases — fossil fuel producers, electric utilities that burn coal and gas, and heavy industry — would benefit, because the bill would remove the legal basis for federal limits on their carbon emissions. Consumers of electricity and fuel could see somewhat lower prices if regulation were blocked, but would bear the health and climate costs of uncontrolled emissions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would add carbon dioxide, water vapor, methane, and chlorofluorocarbons to a list of substances that are not 'air pollutants' under the Clean Air Act, removing them from the EPA's regulatory reach [S2][S3].
It would also declare that nothing in the Clean Air Act authorizes or requires regulation of climate change or global warming, foreclosing greenhouse gas rules under the Act entirely [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the costs of unchecked climate change and unregulated air emissions — including health effects from pollution and long-term climate damages — while polluting industries avoided compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via health and climate harm

drawbacks.text: Blocking EPA greenhouse gas regulation under the Clean Air Act would leave emissions of carbon dioxide, methane, and other gases unaddressed, with public health and climate consequences [S2][S3].
The bill was introduced in the final months of a two-year Congress and referred to committee the same day, making advancement in that session essentially impossible [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a large benefit to emitting industries by eliminating a major regulatory threat, while shifting the costs of pollution and climate change onto the public. It never became law, so its practical effect is nil.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on July 30, 2008, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Marsha Blackburn introduced H.R. 6666 on July 30, 2008, with 25 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and to its Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill died in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill dead, no change was made to the Clean Air Act, so the status quo — including existing EPA authority over air pollutants — was preserved; greenhouse gas-emitting industries did not gain the exemption they sought, and public health and climate regulation was left intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no Clean Air Act change

for.name: Rep. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exclude greenhouse gases from Clean Air Act regulation.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats supported the bill, and no votes were ever taken [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have exempted carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases from Clean Air Act regulation, relieving power plants, refineries, and other large emitters of potential federal limits [S2][S3].
